content: 1. This report provides updated information on the potential adverse events associated with vaccines for hepatitis B, poliomyelitis, measles, mumps, diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. 2. The findings in this report are based on recent literature reviews conducted by an expert committee at the Institute of Medicine (IOM), which examined all available evidence regarding possible adverse consequences of vaccines administered to children. 3. This report includes modifications to previously published recommendations by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), reflecting a review of IOM findings and new research on vaccine safety. 4. Additionally, the report incorporates information from prior ACIP recommendations, such as those on the use of vaccines and immune globulins in immunocompromised individuals and general immunization guidelines. 5. Major changes to previous recommendations are highlighted in the text, with specific details on vaccines and their associated adverse events, including hepatitis B vaccine and anaphylaxis, measles vaccine and thrombocytopenia, and risks of death in immunocompromised individuals. 6. The report also addresses diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTP) vaccines and chronic encephalopathy, as well as tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccines and their association with Guillain-Barré syndrome, brachial neuritis, and anaphylaxis-related risks. 7. These updates will be incorporated into comprehensive ACIP recommendations for each vaccine as new information becomes available. 8. Interim recommendations are included for the use of measles and mumps vaccines in individuals with HIV infection or egg allergies, though ACIP is still evaluating these recommendations. 9. The terms side effects and adverse reactions are used interchangeably in this publication to describe undesirable secondary effects resulting from vaccination. 10. Immunization has led to the global eradication of smallpox, the elimination of poliomyelitis in the Western Hemisphere, and significant reductions in other vaccine-preventable diseases in the United States. 11. Despite the success of immunization, vaccines can cause minor and, rarely, serious side effects. 12. Public awareness and controversy about vaccine safety have increased due to higher vaccine coverage, which has led to more reported adverse events following vaccination. 13. Adverse events include true vaccine reactions and coincidental events unrelated to vaccination. 14. Vaccination remains safer than the risks posed by the diseases it prevents, except in cases where a disease has been eradicated (e.g., smallpox). 15. Failure to vaccinate increases risks to both individuals and society. 16. In response to vaccine safety concerns, the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986 established a no-fault compensation process for individuals potentially injured by vaccines. 17. The Act also mandated that the IOM review scientific evidence regarding possible adverse consequences of vaccines administered to children. 18. The IOM formed an expert committee to review all available information on vaccine adverse events, including epidemiologic studies, case series, individual case reports, and testimonials. 19. The IOM committee categorized causality relationships between vaccines and specific adverse events into five categories. 20. The first IOM review examined events following pertussis and rubella vaccines, while the second review focused on other childhood vaccines, including diphtheria, tetanus, measles, mumps, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and poliovirus vaccines. 21. Subsequent IOM committees have published findings on vaccine-associated adverse events and research strategies for addressing them. 22. The ACIP reviewed IOM findings and updated its recommendations to align with IOM conclusions, ensuring consistency in vaccine safety guidelines. 23. These updated recommendations address precautions, contraindications, side effects, and adverse reactions associated with specific vaccines. 24. The ACIP accepted IOM conclusions and incorporated them into its recommendations, which are included in this report. 25. The report highlights new information on vaccines and adverse events, including hepatitis B vaccine and anaphylaxis, measles vaccine and thrombocytopenia, and risks of death in immunocompromised individuals. 26. Modifications in this report will be integrated into future comprehensive ACIP recommendations as new data become available. 27. Hepatitis B vaccines are safe for adults and children, with millions of doses administered worldwide. 28. Common side effects include pain at the injection site and mild fever, which occur at rates similar to those in placebo-controlled studies. 29. Surveillance has identified a possible association between Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and the first dose of plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccine, though no such association has been found with recombinant vaccines. 30. Anaphylaxis following hepatitis B vaccination is rare but can be life-threatening; subsequent doses are contraindicated for individuals with a history of anaphylaxis to the vaccine. 31. Large-scale hepatitis B immunization programs have not established associations with other severe adverse events, such as seizures or GBS. 32. Any presumed risks of adverse events must be weighed against the significant risks of hepatitis B virus-related liver disease. 33. Surveillance for vaccine-associated adverse events will remain a critical component of immunization programs. 34. Adverse events suspected to be associated with hepatitis B vaccination should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). 35. Poliomyelitis vaccination recommendations have been updated to reflect new findings on adverse events. 36. Oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) is contraindicated in individuals with immune-deficiency diseases due to the risk of vaccine-associated disease. 37. Inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) is recommended for immunodeficient individuals and their household contacts. 38. OPV has been associated with rare cases of paralytic poliomyelitis in healthy recipients and their contacts, as well as fatal cases in immunocompromised individuals. 39. IPV has not been associated with serious side effects, though hypersensitivity reactions may occur in individuals sensitive to trace antibiotics in the vaccine. 40. Measles vaccination has an excellent safety record, with rare adverse events such as fever, rash, and central nervous system conditions occurring at low rates. 41. Febrile seizures following measles vaccination are uncommon and do not increase the risk of epilepsy or other neurologic disorders. 42. The benefits of measles vaccination outweigh the risks, even for children with a personal or family history of seizures. 43. Parents should monitor for fever after vaccination and treat their children appropriately. 44. Antipyretics may help prevent febrile seizures if administered before the onset of fever.
